source.title: Toward Understanding the Transferability of Adversarial Suffixes in Large Language Models
source.authors: Sarah Ball; Niki Hasrati; A. Robey; Avi Schwarzschild; Frauke Kreuter; Zico Kolter; Andrej Risteski

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; it is not visibly garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how GCG suffixes change activations along a refusal direction and relates those changes to jailbreak transfer success, using statistical analyses rather than the original study’s removal/addition interventions. It tests the attack-suppression part of V3, but does not test training against ablation.
record.gate_note: The study defines a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction, but does not ablate or add it to test refusal or general capability (so V1 is not tested). It measures associations between direction-related features and GCG transfer success, and reports rephrasing experiments relating refusal-direction alignment to attack success. The altered-GCG-loss tables report the authors’ attack-method performance and coefficient sweeps, not a result isolating what suppressing the direction itself does; those values are not rows. The human-versus-judge agreement result concerns judge reliability, not the claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures how GCG suffixes shift last-token activations along a difference-in-means refusal direction in four models. It regresses transfer success on that 'suffix push', which bears directly on whether attacks work by suppressing the direction (V3). The evidence is correlational plus a small loss-regularizer intervention. There is no ablation or addition of the direction, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find that suffix push away from the refusal direction is the strongest suffix-side predictor of transfer across models. Prompt refusal connection matters strongly for some models, Vicuna especially. Orthogonal shift is secondary and model-dependent, and semantic similarity is only weakly predictive. They use these insights to design somewhat stronger attacks.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses the refusal direction as a measured feature in GCG attack-transfer analyses; it does not perform the original direction-ablation or direction-addition interventions. It measures activations at an optimal layer, rather than ablating across every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model, intra- versus inter-model transfer direction, and whether features are considered individually or jointly; orthogonal-shift associations change direction in the joint analysis for Vicuna and Llama 2. Semantic-similarity effects vary with embedding source.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompts whose unsuffixed activations align more with the refusal direction are harder to jailbreak with transferred suffixes. This holds in joint models for Qwen, Vicuna and Llama 2 and for Llama 3.2→Qwen, but not for Llama 3.2. Single-feature models show it only for Vicuna. Rephrasing results agree weakly (r=−0.08, −0.18).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A harmful prompt's projection on the refusal direction predicts its resistance to suffix jailbreaks.

fits_no_version.finding: Suffix-induced shifts orthogonal to the refusal direction predict transfer positively when tested alone. In joint models the sign is model-dependent: negative for Vicuna and Llama 2, positive for Qwen and Llama 3.2. These effects are smaller than suffix push.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Successful suffixes also perturb activations off the refusal direction, with a secondary, model-dependent effect.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt semantic similarity weakly predicts suffix transfer (marginal R² 0.000–0.048).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantic similarity between prompts is a weak predictor of GCG suffix transfer.

record.problems: The direction-related feature effects are largely statistical associations, not selective causal interventions on the refusal direction. The study itself notes that the reverse inter-model transfer direction has very low success and insufficient variance for significant feature relationships. Some orthogonal-shift results change sign between single-feature and joint analyses. The excerpt reports significance thresholds but not confidence intervals or standard errors for the regression coefficients.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results omitted. The altered-GCG-loss coefficient sweeps in Tables 4–5 are excluded because they report the performance of the authors’ modified attack method, without a reported measurement that the regularizers actually changed refusal-direction activations. The coefficients are presented as attack-method results and hyperparameter sweeps.

untested.parts: Whether training against direction ablation adds robustness. Attacks other than GCG suffixes. A causal test that suppression alone produces compliance.
Not tested: no ablation or addition of the direction, no capability checks.
Not tested: orthogonal shift is not a claim about refusal's own geometry.
Not tested: inter-model suffix transfer is studied, but not transfer of the direction itself.

missing.what: Qualitative layer-wise result for all four models. The three most successful suffixes strongly reduce cosine similarity with the refusal direction; the three least successful only marginally reduce it.

Interventional result on Llama 3.2: adding a suffix-push regularizer to the GCG loss raises ASR from 0.0138 to 0.0214 at coefficient 0.001, but lowers it to 0.0093 at 0.1. No check that the regularizer changed the projection. A non-monotonic, weak causal hint on V3, worth a row flagged as partial.

record.verdict_notes: The V3 support is correlational: the mixed-effects regressions are not ablations, and only GCG is studied. Vicuna is listed as 14B in the paper's Table 6, although the model is Vicuna-13B-v1.5. States on rows r1–r8 are irrelevant to any version. The judge-agreement result is about judge reliability, not the claim.

versions.untested_parts: No removal or addition of the direction to test refusal, induced refusal on harmless prompts, or preservation of general capabilities.
The study tests GCG suffix attacks and direction-related activation changes, but not whether training against direction ablation adds robustness.
Orthogonal activation shifts are measured as a transfer predictor, but the study does not test or argue that refusal is represented by an affine structure, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
The study evaluates suffix transfer across two models, but does not test whether the refusal direction itself transfers across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
No intervention on refusal-training method or timing to test whether it determines the existence of a removable direction.

relationships.condition: Intra-model GCG transfer in Qwen2.5-3B, Vicuna-13B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.2-1B, plus Llama 3.2→Qwen inter-model transfer
relationships.reason: Greater suffix push away from the refusal direction predicts transfer success, all p<0.001. Single-feature coefficients are 1.28–3.56 (r10, r13, r16, r19); joint coefficients are 1.06–3.61 (r22, r25, r28, r31). Llama 3.2→Qwen gives 1.34 (r34).
relationships.display_finding: Greater displacement predicted transfer with all p<0.001, single-feature coefficients of 1.28–3.56, joint coefficients of 1.06–3.61 and a Llama 3.2-to-Qwen coefficient of 1.34.

source_check.reason: Suffix push is positive and p<0.001 in all four models, both single-feature (1.28–3.56) and joint (1.06–3.61). Llama 3.2→Qwen gives 1.34***. Authors call suffix push the strongest suffix-side factor. Evidence is correlational. V3's adversarial-training half is untested.

relationships.reason: The suffix-push coefficient is −0.99 and not significant (r37). The authors attribute this to very low transfer success in that direction.
relationships.display_finding: The suffix-displacement coefficient was −0.99 and statistically nonsignificant, which the authors attributed to very low transfer success.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Suffix push −0.99 n.s. on N 9,900. The fit is near-degenerate (R2c 0.983, intercept −23.25) and the authors blame insufficient variance from very few successful transfers. An underpowered null does not show V3 needs qualifying; by the letter of the non-significant = absent rule, limits_scope is defensible.

relation.reason: The study's own results (Tables 2, 3, 7 and the GCG-loss intervention) bear on whether suffix attacks work by pushing activations away from the refusal direction.

tranche.reason: Correlational mixed-effects regressions of GCG transfer success on suffix push along a DiM refusal direction. This is a different method aimed at V3's question. Figure 4 qualitatively repeats Arditi's cross-layer suppression plot, but the main results are the regressions.

source_check.notes: The evidence is correlational. The one intervention on Llama 3.2 is a suffix-push regulariser in the GCG loss. It raised ASR from 0.0138 to 0.0214 at coefficient 0.001 but lowered it to 0.0093–0.0101 at 0.1–0.5 (Table 4), so more push is not monotonically better. Vicuna's strongest predictor is prompt refusal connectivity (−4.85 joint), not suffix push.

statements.correction: Qwen→Llama-3.2: suffix push −0.99, n.s., N 9,900, R2m 0.040, R2c 0.983, intercept −23.25; authors say very low transfer success gave insufficient variance. Llama-3.2-1B intra-model: suffix push 1.28*** (single), 1.06*** (joint), the smallest of four models, R2m 0.194 vs 0.495–0.688. Llama-3.2→Qwen: 1.34***.
statements.problem: The numbers and the authors' explanation are right. But this is an underpowered null with very few successful Qwen→Llama-3.2 transfers. It is not evidence that suppression-based attacks work unevenly across families. The same study finds significant suffix-push effects for Llama-3.2-1B elsewhere.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The study reports statistical associations and prompt-rephrasing correlations rather than an intervention that selectively removes the refusal direction; these results do not establish that direction suppression alone causes attack success. See r10–r20, r22–r32, and r39–r40.
